screens.title: Implementing 3D Character Controllers & Input
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll bring a player to life in a 3D scene by choosing the right movement approach, wiring input, and building a follow camera that feels responsive. You'll learn the difference between Unity's built-in CharacterController, which gives precise, programmatic movement and handles collision sliding, and a Rigidbody-based controller that uses physics for realistic interactions. We'll walk through a basic script that reads player input, applies manual gravity and jump impulses, then show how a camera target and smoothing create a natural third-person view. You'll also see common pitfalls: forgetting to apply gravity with a CharacterController, or updating physics in the wrong loop with a Rigidbody. By the end you'll understand how to match technique to gameplay needs, how to map actions to keyboard and gamepad using Input Actions, and how to keep the camera from clipping into geometry. Think of this chapter as the bridge between raw input and playable character feeling — we'll focus on code examples you can copy, test, and iterate on, and on a handful of best practices that prevent the usual surprises.

Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Implementing 3D Character Controllers & Input
Implementing 3D Character Controllers & Input
Understand movement approaches, map input declaratively, and craft a following camera that stays readable in gameplay.
In this lesson
Compare CharacterController vs Rigidbody, implement a PlayerMovement script, and wire a ThirdPersonCamera with smoothing and collision protection.
Why it matters
Movement and camera directly affect feel and player control. Choosing the right system avoids floating characters, jitter, and unwanted physics interactions during gameplay.
Explore key topics
CharacterController
Script-driven moves with built-in collision sliding and manual gravity.
Rigidbody Movement
Physics-driven response that reacts to forces and other dynamic objects.
Third-Person Camera
Follow, smooth, and avoid clipping using LateUpdate and raycasts.
Concept Preview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Play loop
Input → Movement logic → Collision resolution → Camera follow. Tuning any step changes the player feel.
Input
Input Actions or WASD map to Move and Jump behaviors.
Output
Character velocity and camera position produce on-screen motion.
Quick tip
Start with CharacterController for predictable movement. Move to Rigidbody when you need physical pushes, explosions, or realistic momentum.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This set of objectives defines the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will be able to differentiate between Unity's CharacterController and a custom physics-based controller. That means recognizing when you need precise, script-driven movement versus when you must let the physics engine influence the player, and describing the trade-offs. Second, you'll implement basic 3D movement: walking, running, and jumping using a C# script. You'll write code that reads input, applies movement vectors, and adds gravity so characters don't float after a jump. Third, you'll develop a responsive third-person camera that follows the player and lets the user rotate the view. You'll use LateUpdate and smoothing functions to avoid jitter and create a natural feel. Fourth, you'll identify common challenges such as collision edge cases, slope handling, and update-loop mistakes, and propose solutions like adjusting slopeLimit, using FixedUpdate for physics, or raycasting to prevent camera clipping. Each objective is tied to an actionable milestone so you can test and verify the competency in a small playtest scene.

screens.title: CharacterController: definition and behavior
screens.narratorSegment: The CharacterController is a Unity component focused on player characters that performs collision detection and sliding without relying on the physics engine to drive motion. In practice this means you call Move or SimpleMove with a movement vector and the controller computes collisions and prevents penetration. Gravity and vertical velocity are not applied automatically in the physics sense; you must add a downward term to the movement vector each frame. A concrete example: when you press forward, your script computes a world-space direction relative to the camera and multiplies it by a move speed, then adds the current vertical velocity before calling Move. If you forget to apply gravity, the player will float after a jump — a common mistake. The CharacterController exposes adjustable properties like slopeLimit and stepOffset. Use slopeLimit to control the maximum incline the character can climb and stepOffset to allow stepping up small ledges. These parameters let you tune traversal so players cross small obstacles but can't climb sheer walls. A misconception is that CharacterController gives physics responses; it does not react to forces from other rigidbodies. Use it when you want precise, deterministic control rather than physically realistic pushes.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › CharacterController: definition
Core Concept
CharacterController behavior
A non-physics-driven mover that handles collisions and sliding. You supply movement vectors; it prevents penetration and steps over small obstacles when tuned.
Key properties
  • slopeLimit: controls maximum climbable incline.
  • stepOffset: allows automatic stepping up small ledges.
  • isGrounded: reports whether controller touches ground.
Common mistake
Forgetting manual gravity makes the character float after jump. Always add a vertical velocity term to movement before Move().
Walkthrough: how movement works
The script computes a desired horizontal vector relative to camera orientation, normalizes it, scales by speed, then combines it with verticalVelocity and calls controller.Move(delta).
<!-- Example pseudocode flow, not exact code --> desired = normalized(camera.forward * v + camera.right * h) * speed if grounded and jumpPressed: verticalVelocity = jumpForce else: verticalVelocity += gravity * deltaTime movement = desired + Vector3.up * verticalVelocity controller.Move(movement * deltaTime)
Example
A platformer uses CharacterController for tight, non-slippery movement and well-controlled jumps.
Takeaway
CharacterController = deterministic control, manual gravity, adjustable slope/step tuning.

screens.title: Setting up CharacterController and movement script
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up a playable CharacterController scene follows a clear sequence you can repeat for every player character. Start by creating a Capsule GameObject and adding a CharacterController component. Adjust the controller's Height and Radius to fit the visual mesh so collision aligns with the model. Next create a PlayerMovement C# script and attach it to the same GameObject. In the script's Start method confirm the CharacterController component exists and disable the script if it doesn't — this prevents null-reference errors during play. In Update, read horizontal and vertical input axes or Input Actions mapped to a Move behavior. Convert that input into a world-space direction by using the camera's forward and right vectors with their y components set to zero, so movement remains horizontal. Normalize and multiply by moveSpeed. Handle grounding with controller. isGrounded: when grounded, reset small negative vertical velocity; when not, accumulate gravity into verticalVelocity. For jumping, check for a Jump action and set verticalVelocity to jumpForce when grounded. Finally, combine horizontal and vertical into a movement vector and call controller. Move(movement * Time. deltaTime). This order ensures collision is computed each frame and that gravity keeps the player grounded.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Controller Setup
Step-by-step
  1. Create a Capsule and rename to Player. Add CharacterController and match height/radius to model.
  2. Create PlayerMovement script and attach it. In Start, cache controller reference and disable if missing.
  3. In Update read Move input, compute camera-relative forward and right, zero out y, normalize, apply moveSpeed.
  4. Handle grounding via controller.isGrounded, apply manual gravity each frame, and set jump impulse when requested.
  5. Combine horizontal and vertical motion, call controller.Move(movement * Time.deltaTime).
Pro tip
Use a small negative vertical velocity when grounded to keep the controller snapped to slopes and avoid floating.
Visual checklist and example
A short run through to verify each step in the editor and play mode.
<!-- Example code snippet (escaped) --> using UnityEngine; public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour { public float moveSpeed = 5f; public float jumpForce = 8f; public float gravity = -20f; private CharacterController controller; private float verticalVelocity; void Start() { controller = GetComponent<CharacterController>(); if (controller == null) { enabled = false; } } void Update() { /* compute input, gravity, and controller.Move() here */ } }
Example test
Press WASD and Space: character should walk and jump then return to ground without drifting.
Pitfall
Calling controller.Move with incorrect delta scaling can produce inconsistent speeds across frame rates; multiply by Time.deltaTime.

screens.title: Rigidbody-based controllers vs CharacterController
screens.narratorSegment: A Rigidbody-based controller hands movement to the physics engine so the player becomes an active participant in physical interactions like pushes, explosions, and realistic momentum. Implementing this involves attaching a Rigidbody to the player and using methods such as setting Rigidbody. velocity, Rigidbody. AddForce, or Rigidbody. MovePosition to move. The main advantage is authentic reactions to external forces. A concrete example: a rolling boulder should push the player if they collide. However, this realism comes with trade-offs — directly setting velocity every frame can produce jitter, especially if done in Update rather than FixedUpdate. A best practice is to apply forces or adjust velocity in FixedUpdate so physics calculations stay consistent with the physics timestep. Another common challenge is controlling friction and sliding; you may need to tune constraints, mass, drag, or use physics materials to reduce unwanted sliding. When you need precise platforming or instant, non-slippery input response, CharacterController often gives a better result. When physical interactions and momentum matter for gameplay mechanics, prefer Rigidbody and design your movement code to cooperate with Unity's physics loop. Rigidbody-based controllers vs CharacterController means rigidbody offers realistic interactions but requires physics-aware code in fixedupdate and careful tuning to avoid jitter and unwanted sliding.. In practical terms, when to use physics-driven movement and how it changes control. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › Rigidbody vs CharacterController
Quick comparison
CharacterController
Precise, script-driven movement. Manual gravity. No physical pushes from other rigidbodies.
Rigidbody
Physics-driven, reacts to forces and collisions, uses FixedUpdate for consistent behavior.
When to choose
  • Choose CharacterController for tight platforming and deterministic control.
  • Choose Rigidbody when environmental physics must affect the player.
Practical tips for Rigidbody
  • Apply forces or change velocity inside FixedUpdate to match the physics timestep.
  • Use ForceMode.VelocityChange for immediate velocity adjustments without mass scaling.
  • Tune mass, drag, and physics materials to reduce sliding while preserving responsiveness.
<!-- Example usage (escaped) --> void FixedUpdate() { Vector3 desired = // compute movement rigidbody.AddForce(desired * speed, ForceMode.VelocityChange); }
Example
Use Rigidbody when a falling crate should knock the player back and change their velocity.
Misconception
Rigidbody does not automatically make control better; it makes interactions realistic but requires extra tuning for player feel.

screens.title: PlayerMovement script explained
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a minimal PlayerMovement script to show the essential parts and the meaning behind each line. The script exposes moveSpeed, jumpForce, and a custom gravity so you can tune feel without changing global physics. In Start we cache the CharacterController reference and disable the script if the component is missing — a quick safety measure. Each frame in Update we first read horizontal and vertical inputs or Input Actions, then compute camera-relative forward and right vectors with their vertical components zeroed so movement stays on the ground plane. Normalizing the combined vector preserves consistent diagonal speed. The gravity term accumulates into verticalVelocity each frame; when grounded and verticalVelocity is slightly negative we snap it to a small downward value to keep the controller grounded. For jumping we detect the Jump action and set verticalVelocity to jumpForce if grounded. Finally we combine horizontal movement and verticalVelocity into one Vector3 and call controller. Move with Time. deltaTime scaling. A concrete debugging tip: if the player floats after jumping, check that verticalVelocity receives gravity each frame and that controller. Move is multiplied by delta time.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › PlayerMovement walkthrough
Full example (escaped for display)
// Example: Basic PlayerMovement
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    public float jumpForce = 8f;
    public float gravity = -20f; // Custom gravity for CharacterController

    private CharacterController controller;
    private Vector3 moveDirection;
    private float verticalVelocity;
    private bool isGrounded;

    void Start()
    {
        controller = GetComponent<CharacterController>();
        if (controller == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("CharacterController not found on this GameObject.");
            enabled = false; // Disable script if no controller
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        // Movement, gravity, and controller.Move called here
    }
}
The snippet above shows the structure: public tuning fields, cached controller, and space for Update logic. Keep physics state like verticalVelocity inside the script so jumps behave consistently.
Explanation cards
Gravity handling
Accumulate gravity into verticalVelocity each frame and include it in the movement vector so the controller falls naturally.
Camera-relative movement
Compute forward and right from the main camera with y=0 so forward input moves toward where the player is looking horizontally.
Grounding trick
When grounded and verticalVelocity is negative, set it to a small negative value to keep contact with uneven terrain.
Check your understanding
Why must gravity be applied manually with CharacterController, and what happens if you apply it in FixedUpdate instead of Update?

screens.title: ThirdPersonCamera script walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: A responsive third-person camera typically reads rotation input, computes a desired position behind a CameraTarget, and then moves smoothly while looking at the target. The provided ThirdPersonCamera script stores the rotation angles currentX and currentY and updates them with mouse input multiplied by a rotationSpeed. Clamping currentY prevents the camera from rotating under the ground or flipping over the player. In LateUpdate, we compute a Quaternion from the angles and apply it to calculate the desired position as the target position minus the forward vector times distance, plus an upward offset. Using Vector3. Lerp or SmoothDamp to interpolate the camera position produces smooth transitions instead of jarring jumps, improving perceived stability. The script then calls transform. LookAt so the camera focuses on the target. A practical improvement is adding a raycast from target to desired position; if the ray hits an obstacle, place the camera at the hit point to avoid clipping through geometry. A common misconception is that Update is fine for camera movement — but LateUpdate ensures the camera moves after the player, preventing visible lag or jitter when the player moves in Update.

keyIdea.title: Camera pattern
keyIdea.text: Use LateUpdate to follow a CameraTarget, rotate using input with clamped pitch, smooth position with Lerp, and protect from clipping with raycasts.

content.html:
Module 04 › Chapter 4.2 › ThirdPersonCamera walkthrough
Full script (escaped)
// ThirdPersonCamera.cs
using UnityEngine;

public class ThirdPersonCamera : MonoBehaviour
{
    public Transform target; // Assign CameraTarget here
    public float distance = 5.0f;
    public float height = 2.0f;
    public float rotationSpeed = 3.0f;
    public float smoothSpeed = 0.125f;

    private float currentX = 0.0f;
    private float currentY = 0.0f;

    void LateUpdate()
    {
        if (target == null) return;

        currentX += Input.GetAxis("Mouse X") * rotationSpeed;
        currentY -= Input.GetAxis("Mouse Y") * rotationSpeed;
        currentY = Mathf.Clamp(currentY, -30f, 60f);

        Quaternion rotation = Quaternion.Euler(currentY, currentX, 0);
        Vector3 desiredPosition = target.position - rotation * Vector3.forward * distance + Vector3.up * height;
        Vector3 smoothedPosition = Vector3.Lerp(transform.position, desiredPosition, smoothSpeed);
        transform.position = smoothedPosition;
        transform.LookAt(target.position);
    }
}
This script demonstrates the common follow-and-look pattern. Clamping and smoothing parameters are the primary levers for feel.
Explanation cards
LateUpdate
Ensures the camera updates after player movement so the view matches the final character position for the frame.
Smoothing
Use Lerp or SmoothDamp for smooth motion; adjust smoothSpeed to control follow tightness.
Collision protection
Raycast from target to desired position and move camera to hit point to avoid clipping through walls.
Challenge
Adjust rotationSpeed and smoothSpeed so camera feels natural for both slow walking and quick turns.

screens.title: Input handling: Legacy vs New Input System
screens.narratorSegment: Handling player input cleanly makes your movement code device-agnostic and easier to maintain. The legacy Input Manager uses functions like GetAxis and GetButton, which work but become cumbersome when supporting many devices or remapping controls. The new Input System encourages defining Input Actions such as Move, Jump, and Look, then binding them to multiple devices like keyboard keys, mouse delta, or gamepad sticks. In practice you create an Input Actions asset, define a Move action that reads a two-dimensional vector, and bind WASD and the left stick to it. In code you subscribe to action events or read the action's current value in Update. This modular approach keeps input logic out of gameplay code and makes switching devices seamless. A concrete example: bind Move to WASD and the left stick; the same code will read a Vector2 regardless of device. A common misconception is that the new system is strictly event-only; it supports both callbacks and polling so you can integrate it into existing Update loops. By mapping behaviors to actions, you make movement scripts focused on intent — move, jump, look — not the raw keys themselves.

Example use:

New Input System
Define Input Actions like Move and Jump and bind them to multiple devices. Use callbacks or poll action values in Update.

Input Actions let you change bindings without touching movement code and make cross-device support straightforward.
Tip
Start with actions named for intent, not keys: Move, Jump, Look, Sprint.

screens.title: Camera and Player relationship
screens.narratorSegment: Designing the relationship between player and camera begins by separating responsibilities. Rather than moving the camera directly based on player models, create a CameraTarget transform as a child of the Player. Position this target a bit behind and above the head so the camera focuses on an appropriate point for framing. The camera script references this target and updates its own position in LateUpdate so it follows after the player's movement logic has run. Using an intermediate CameraTarget makes it easy to add aim offsets, crouch adjustments, or look-at targets later without editing camera math. For smoothness, calculate a desired position from the target using rotation and distance, then interpolate the camera toward it. To avoid clipping into geometry, perform a raycast from the target to the desired camera position; if it hits, place the camera at the hit point, slightly in front of the obstacle. A misconception is parenting the camera directly to the player for all motion — that often causes camera shake or unfiltered rotation. Keep the camera as a separate object that follows and looks at the CameraTarget for predictable and tuneable framing.

Component roles

  • CameraTarget: a transform offset for framing that the camera looks at.
  • Camera: separate GameObject that follows target in LateUpdate and smooths position.
Why a target
It isolates camera concerns and gives a single anchor for look-at and collision checks, simplifying future adjustments like aim offsets.
Collision avoidance pattern
Raycast from CameraTarget to desired camera position. If hit, move camera to hit point minus a short buffer distance. If not hit, use smoothed desired position.
Example
Raycast detects a wall; camera pulls closer so the player remains visible without seeing inside geometry.
Takeaway
Keep camera logic decoupled and update it after player movement to avoid visual inconsistencies.

screens.title: Common problems and fixes
screens.narratorSegment: When implementing movement and camera systems you will encounter a handful of repeatable issues. One is the floating character: this happens when gravity is not applied every frame to a CharacterController or when the grounding check is unreliable. Fix it by ensuring verticalVelocity accumulates gravity in Update and by resetting verticalVelocity to a small negative value when controller. isGrounded is true. Another problem is jittery Rigidbody movement. If you set velocity or apply forces in Update, physics will feel inconsistent; move those changes into FixedUpdate so the physics engine processes them at a fixed timestep. Camera clipping occurs when the camera moves into environment geometry; a raycast from the CameraTarget to the desired camera position will reveal obstacles and let you reposition the camera at the hit point. Also watch for inconsistent input values across devices — test with keyboard and gamepad to tune dead zones and sensitivities. A common misconception is blaming the camera script for all motion issues; often jitter originates from mismatch between Update and LateUpdate or incorrect delta-time usage. Use the playtest checklist: gravity, FixedUpdate for physics, clamped rotation, and raycast camera checks.

Symptoms and fixes
Floating after jump
Cause: gravity not applied or isGrounded check incorrect. Fix: accumulate gravity into verticalVelocity each Update and set a small negative value when grounded.
Jittery Rigidbody movement
Cause: physics changes in Update. Fix: apply forces and velocity changes in FixedUpdate to align with physics timestep.

Cause: desired camera position intersects geometry. Fix: raycast from target to desired position and reposition camera to the hit point minus a small offset.

In this lesson we'll bring a player to life in a 3D scene by choosing the right movement approach, wiring input, and building a follow camera that feels responsive. You'll learn the difference between Unity's built-in CharacterController, which gives precise, programmatic movement and handles collision sliding, and a Rigidbody-based controller that uses physics for realistic interactions. We'll walk through a basic script that reads player input, applies manual gravity and jump impulses, then show how a camera target and smoothing create a natural third-person view. You'll also see common pitfalls: forgetting to apply gravity with a CharacterController, or updating physics in the wrong loop with a Rigidbody. By the end you'll understand how to match technique to gameplay needs, how to map actions to keyboard and gamepad using Input Actions, and how to keep the camera from clipping into geometry. Think of this chapter as the bridge between raw input and playable character feeling — we'll focus on code examples you can copy, test, and iterate on, and on a handful of best practices that prevent the usual surprises.

This set of objectives defines the practical skills you'll gain. First, you will be able to differentiate between Unity's CharacterController and a custom physics-based controller. That means recognizing when you need precise, script-driven movement versus when you must let the physics engine influence the player, and describing the trade-offs. Second, you'll implement basic 3D movement: walking, running, and jumping using a C# script. You'll write code that reads input, applies movement vectors, and adds gravity so characters don't float after a jump. Third, you'll develop a responsive third-person camera that follows the player and lets the user rotate the view. You'll use LateUpdate and smoothing functions to avoid jitter and create a natural feel. Fourth, you'll identify common challenges such as collision edge cases, slope handling, and update-loop mistakes, and propose solutions like adjusting slopeLimit, using FixedUpdate for physics, or raycasting to prevent camera clipping. Each objective is tied to an actionable milestone so you can test and verify the competency in a small playtest scene.

This companion objectives slide ties each learning target to a hands-on implementation. For differentiating movement systems, you'll set up two simple scenes: one where the player uses CharacterController to walk and step over small obstacles, and another where a Rigidbody player is pushed by a rolling object to observe physics interactions. For implementing movement, you'll write a PlayerMovement script that reads a Move action, translates it relative to the camera, applies a configurable moveSpeed, and applies a manual gravity term with a small downward bias while grounding. For the camera objective, you'll create a CameraTarget child on the player and implement a ThirdPersonCamera script that reads mouse input for rotation, clamps vertical angles, and smooths position with Lerp. For diagnosing issues, you'll run playtests to reproduce common mistakes — forgetting gravity, updating physics in Update, or neglecting camera collision checks — and then apply known remedies. Each objective includes a small milestone you can verify: character stays grounded after jump, camera avoids clipping, and physics pushes affect the Rigidbody-based player.

The CharacterController is a Unity component focused on player characters that performs collision detection and sliding without relying on the physics engine to drive motion. In practice this means you call Move or SimpleMove with a movement vector and the controller computes collisions and prevents penetration. Gravity and vertical velocity are not applied automatically in the physics sense; you must add a downward term to the movement vector each frame. A concrete example: when you press forward, your script computes a world-space direction relative to the camera and multiplies it by a move speed, then adds the current vertical velocity before calling Move. If you forget to apply gravity, the player will float after a jump — a common mistake. The CharacterController exposes adjustable properties like slopeLimit and stepOffset. Use slopeLimit to control the maximum incline the character can climb and stepOffset to allow stepping up small ledges. These parameters let you tune traversal so players cross small obstacles but can't climb sheer walls. A misconception is that CharacterController gives physics responses; it does not react to forces from other rigidbodies. Use it when you want precise, deterministic control rather than physically realistic pushes.

Setting up a playable CharacterController scene follows a clear sequence you can repeat for every player character. Start by creating a Capsule GameObject and adding a CharacterController component. Adjust the controller's Height and Radius to fit the visual mesh so collision aligns with the model. Next create a PlayerMovement C# script and attach it to the same GameObject. In the script's Start method confirm the CharacterController component exists and disable the script if it doesn't — this prevents null-reference errors during play. In Update, read horizontal and vertical input axes or Input Actions mapped to a Move behavior. Convert that input into a world-space direction by using the camera's forward and right vectors with their y components set to zero, so movement remains horizontal. Normalize and multiply by moveSpeed. Handle grounding with controller. isGrounded: when grounded, reset small negative vertical velocity; when not, accumulate gravity into verticalVelocity. For jumping, check for a Jump action and set verticalVelocity to jumpForce when grounded. Finally, combine horizontal and vertical into a movement vector and call controller. Move(movement * Time. deltaTime). This order ensures collision is computed each frame and that gravity keeps the player grounded.

A Rigidbody-based controller hands movement to the physics engine so the player becomes an active participant in physical interactions like pushes, explosions, and realistic momentum. Implementing this involves attaching a Rigidbody to the player and using methods such as setting Rigidbody. velocity, Rigidbody. AddForce, or Rigidbody. MovePosition to move. The main advantage is authentic reactions to external forces. A concrete example: a rolling boulder should push the player if they collide. However, this realism comes with trade-offs — directly setting velocity every frame can produce jitter, especially if done in Update rather than FixedUpdate. A best practice is to apply forces or adjust velocity in FixedUpdate so physics calculations stay consistent with the physics timestep. Another common challenge is controlling friction and sliding; you may need to tune constraints, mass, drag, or use physics materials to reduce unwanted sliding. When you need precise platforming or instant, non-slippery input response, CharacterController often gives a better result. When physical interactions and momentum matter for gameplay mechanics, prefer Rigidbody and design your movement code to cooperate with Unity's physics loop. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The script exposes moveSpeed, jumpForce, and a custom gravity so you can tune feel without changing global physics. For jumping we detect the Jump action and set verticalVelocity to jumpForce if grounded. Finally we combine horizontal movement and verticalVelocity into one Vector3 and call controller. Move is multiplied by delta time.

A responsive third-person camera typically reads rotation input, computes a desired position behind a CameraTarget, and then moves smoothly while looking at the target. The provided ThirdPersonCamera script stores the rotation angles currentX and currentY and updates them with mouse input multiplied by a rotationSpeed. Clamping currentY prevents the camera from rotating under the ground or flipping over the player. In LateUpdate, we compute a Quaternion from the angles and apply it to calculate the desired position as the target position minus the forward vector times distance, plus an upward offset. Using Vector3. Lerp or SmoothDamp to interpolate the camera position produces smooth transitions instead of jarring jumps, improving perceived stability. The script then calls transform. A practical improvement is adding a raycast from target to desired position; if the ray hits an obstacle, place the camera at the hit point to avoid clipping through geometry. A common misconception is that Update is fine for camera movement — but LateUpdate ensures the camera moves after the player, preventing visible lag or jitter when the player moves in Update.

The legacy Input Manager uses functions like GetAxis and GetButton, which work but become cumbersome when supporting many devices or remapping controls. A concrete example: bind Move to WASD and the left stick; the same code will read a Vector2 regardless of device. A common misconception is that the new system is strictly event-only; it supports both callbacks and polling so you can integrate it into existing Update loops. By mapping behaviors to actions, you make movement scripts focused on intent — move, jump, look — not the raw keys themselves.
